While traditionally viewed as a passive ischemic event, the precise radiogenomic drivers and spatial immune architectures orchestrating active tumor necrosis remain poorly understood. Methods: We integrated macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics with public genomic datasets (n=3,639), single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and high-resolution protein immunofluorescence (IF) assays in a novel co-mutant murine model to map the necrotic microenvironment. Results: Radiomic analysis of patient MRIs demonstrated that high tumoral necrotic volume serves as a powerful independent biomarker for poor long-term survival. This macro-structural necrosis phenotype is radiogenomically driven by cell-intrinsic TP53, PTEN, and NF1 (PPN) co-mutations. Spatial transcriptomic profiling of PPN-deficient tumors revealed distinct cellular topography, separating a proliferative, invasive niche (EGFR+ SOX+, TypeInv) from a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche (ERBB3+, TypeNec). Mechanistically, TypeNec cells deploy a prominent CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine milieu that actively recruits and prompts tumor-associated neutrophils to undergo neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. This overactive neutrophil infiltrate drives a feed-forward loop of intrinsic tumor necroptosis mediated by the release of the damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) protein HMGB2. This cascade could be therapeutically dismantled using targeted anti-inflammatory compounds. Finally, multi-cohort clinical validation confirmed that an HMGB2high signature dictates a high-risk, myeloid-rich immunosuppressive microenvironment in glioblastoma patients. Conclusions: Our findings redefine glioblastoma necrosis as an active, mutation-driven immunopathological process. The HMGB2-mediated DAMP necroptosis cascade and associated myeloid chemokines provide robust prognostic biomarkers and immediate therapeutic vulnerabilities to disrupt the immunosuppressive necrotic niche.

items.title: The ACVR1C-GAS6 Antagonistic Axis Drives Metabolic Decompensation and Liver Fibrosis in MASLD: Mechanistic Insights from Multi-omics Analyses
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide, and liver fibrosis stage is the strongest determinant of long-term morbidity and mortality in affected patients. However, the molecular switches driving the transition from compensated steatosis to progressive fibrogenesis remain poorly characterized, limiting the development of early diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic interventions. Methods We integrated machine learning-based bulk transcriptome screening, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomic validation, and transcriptional regulatory network analysis to systematically dissect the functional roles and interplay of ACVR1C and GAS6 during MASLD progression. Results We identified the ACVR1C-GAS6 antagonistic axis as a central regulatory hub governing hepatocyte metabolic homeostasis and macrophage functional polarization. ACVR1C exerts a previously unrecognized homeostatic gatekeeper role in sustaining hepatocyte detoxification pathways, whereas GAS6 is progressively upregulated across fibrosis stages with a distinct expression threshold marking fibrogenesis onset. Mechanistically, GAS6 drives polarization of heme-related macrophages via the MERTK-STAT3 cascade, which synergizes with direct hepatic stellate cell activation to promote liver fibrosis through a dual pathway. Spatial transcriptomic analysis in a mouse MASLD model further confirmed enhanced in situ co-localization of Gas6 and Mertk in diseased liver tissue. Conclusions The ACVR1C-GAS6 axis provides a novel molecular framework for understanding MASLD progression, and represents promising candidate biomarkers for disease risk stratification and therapeutic targets for clinical translation.

items.title: Machine learning based on non-contrast chest CT radiomics for identifying hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: development and external validation
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) carry a substantial, frequently under-recognized burden of coronary artery disease, yet systematic screening with coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is impractical. We developed and externally validated machine learning models based on radiomics features from routine non-contrast chest CT, combined with clinical variables and quantitative airway parameters, to identify hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis (HSCS) in patients with COPD. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 455 patients with COPD who underwent paired non-contrast chest CT and CCTA between June 2021 and December 2025 (internal cohort, randomly split 7:3 into training [n = 318] and test [n = 137] sets) and 332 patients from an independent external validation cohort. HSCS was defined as ≥ 70% luminal stenosis in at least one major epicardial coronary artery. Whole-lung radiomics features (n = 1688) were extracted with PyRadiomics; after redundancy removal and univariate filtering within the training set, a radiomics score (Rad-score) was built with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression. Clinical and combined models were constructed with five algorithms, including logistic regression, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, random forest, and light gradient boosting machine. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], DeLong tests), calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow test, calibration slope), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis) were assessed, and a nomogram was constructed. Results Age, smoking, diabetes, and a lower airway surface-area-to-volume ratio were independently associated with HSCS. Seventeen radiomics features constituted the Rad-score. The logistic regression combined model achieved AUCs of 0.854 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.802–0.906) in the training set, 0.823 (0.746–0.900) in the internal test set, and 0.798 (0.746–0.851) in the external cohort, significantly outperforming the clinical model (DeLong p = 0.008 and p = 0.002, respectively), with satisfactory calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.749 and 0.189) and superior net benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.05–0.50. Conclusions A machine learning model based on non-contrast chest CT radiomics identifies HSCS in patients with COPD with good, externally validated performance and may support opportunistic cardiovascular risk stratification without additional radiation or contrast exposure.

items.title: Certified Tool Execution Framework for MCP-Based AI Agents: Provably Secure Defense Against Tool Poisoning and Credential Theft
items.abstract_or_text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as the de facto standard for enabling Large Language Model (LLM) agents to interact with external tools, APIs, and databases. While MCP significantly extends agent capabilities, it introduces critical security vulnerabilities: tool poisoning attacks can inject malicious behavior into seemingly benign tools, and prompt injection can trick agents into leaking credentials or performing unauthorized actions. Current defense mechanisms—including prompt filtering, guardrails, and adversarial training—are heuristic and bypassable, with reported evasion rates reaching 100% against state-of-the-art systems.We present the Certified Tool Execution Framework (CTEF), the first provably secure defense against tool poisoning in MCP-based AI agents. CTEF employs a three-layer architecture: (1) capability-based access control (CAP-MCP) that enforces cryptographically unforgeable permissions, (2) formal pre/post-condition verification using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers, and (3) sandboxed execution with syscall-level monitoring. We prove that CTEF achieves (ε, δ)-certified security, where ε < 2-128 represents the probability of accepting a poisoned tool and δ bounds the capability forgery risk.Through comprehensive evaluation on the MCP-Security benchmark comprising 50 benign and 30 poisoned tools across 6 attack categories, CTEF achieves 96.7% true positive rate and 3.2% false positive rate in poisoned tool detection—a 47% improvement over the next-best baseline. We establish theoretical sample complexity bounds showing that detecting a poisoned tool with violation probability, p requires Ω(1/p log 1/δ) samples. The framework incurs 2.3--8.7x execution overhead compared to unprotected MCP, acceptable for security-critical applications. CTEF enables safe deployment of autonomous AI agents in domains where tool integrity is paramount: healthcare decision support, financial trading, infrastructure management, and legal document processing. Our open-source implementation and benchmark are available on [anonymized for review].

items.title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

items.title: Predicting clonal mutations from tumour spatial transcriptomics data using a graph convolutional neural network
items.abstract_or_text: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has revolutionized our understanding of tumour biology but inherently lacks information on the upstream somatic driver mutations. We developed a spatially-aware graph convolutional neural network approach (SPOT-Mut) that infers mutated (sub)clones directly from ST data. SPOT-Mut was trained on virtual ST slides with clones simulated from a large collection of existing RNA and matched DNA sequencing data. SPOT-Mut was first evaluated for predicting mutations in TP53, the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer. Precision and recall values exceeded 95% in most analysed cancer types and the model was validated on ST and matched DNA sequencing data from serial slices obtained from cutaneous SCC samples. SPOT-Mut was then trained on 62 frequently mutated driver genes, resulting in highly performing somatic mutation prediction models for 40 driver genes, including KRAS, KEAP1, CTNNB1 and APC. With the increasing availability of ST data and upcoming atlases, SPOT-Mut potentiates the localization of (sub)clonal alterations in TP53 and other common driver mutations.

items.title: Single-Nucleus Profiling Reveals Neuronal Metabolic Collapse During the Transition to Alzheimer's Disease Dementia
items.abstract_or_text: Current Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathological metrics, including Thal phasing, and Braak staging, often do not accurately predict cognitive status: many cognitively resilient individuals have substantial pathological burdens, whereas some patients with dementia show minimal classical AD pathology. Here, we addressed this discrepancy by investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying AD dementia using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and single-nucleus multiome datasets. To eliminate cross-modality scaling artifacts and compositional biases inherent in neurodegenerative tissues, we normalized the datasets using our novel framework, bypassing scaling issues of conventional methods that may obscure critical biological signals of interest. We identified neuron-specific suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and their upstream mitochondrial biogenesis signaling (MBS) as primary drivers of clinical dementia. By integrating multi-omic quantitative trait loci, genome-wide association studies, and epigenomic profiles, we delineated genetic and epigenetic changes underlying MBS suppression. This study provides a systematic genomic framework for understanding the mechanisms of cognitive resilience.

items.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
items.abstract_or_text: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

items.title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.

items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation
items.abstract_or_text: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.

items.title: The Pedigree Is Not the Pathology: Familial Liability, Addiction-Associated Neuroadaptation and Behavioural Dysregulation in Medical Trainees
items.abstract_or_text: Behavioural dysregulation in medical trainees may coexist with familial vulnerability, substance exposure and altered neural function, yet their concurrence does not establish a common neuropathological cause. Familial aggregation cannot independently distinguish inherited liability from genetic nurture; molecular neuroadaptation cannot establish individual-level behavioural causation; and neuroimaging abnormalities are not equivalent to histopathological lesions. This critical narrative review examines these evidentiary boundaries and proposes FENCE-MED (Familial Liability, Exposure, Neuroadaptation, Circuit Concordance and Evidence-Based Intervention in Medical Education), a falsifiable framework for evaluating mechanistic attribution and clinical utility. Unlike integrative models describing genetic and neurobiological pathways of addiction, FENCE-MED specifies conditions under which familial, molecular and clinical findings may corroborate, contradict or fail to resolve a proposed causal mechanism. Its components include genetically informed family designs, substance-specific longitudinal exposure assessment, graded neuropathological evidence, an uncertainty-aware discordance matrix and prespecified causal and predictive validation. A prospective research architecture is outlined using independently assessed functional impairment, repeated psychiatric phenotyping, selected mechanistic substudies and external validation. The corresponding clinical pathway prioritises confidential assessment, established addiction treatments and demonstrable functional recovery without employing genetic or molecular findings for educational or disciplinary classification. FENCE-MED is neither a diagnostic instrument nor an established preventive intervention. Its proposed contribution is an explicit, testable boundary between inherited susceptibility, addiction-associated neural change, causal explanation and clinically justified action.

items.title: An Upgraded Arsenic Trioxide–Based Salvage Regimen for Relapsed or Refractory Neuroblastoma: Improved Disease Control and Genomic Alterations
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background: Treatment options for children with relapsed or refractory neuroblastoma (NB) remain limited, and objective response rates (ORR) to conventional salvage chemotherapy generally range from 6% to 64%. Arsenic trioxide (ATO) has shown antitumor activity against NB in preclinical and clinical studies. We evaluated the ORR and disease control rate (DCR) of ATO-based salvage chemotherapy in children with relapsed or refractory NB, focusing on the comparison between the original and the upgraded regimen versions and on the response conversion between the two-cycle and four-cycle assessments. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 27 children with relapsed or refractory NB who received ATO-based salvage chemotherapy at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital between January 2024 and August 2025; 26 were evaluable for efficacy. The protocol comprised two regimens (A and B), each encompassing two sub-regimens (A1/A2 and B1/B2); each cycle administered one of them, and the sequence was individualized according to response and tolerability. Patients were classified into the original (n = 15) and upgraded (n = 11) regimen groups. Response was assessed every two cycles according to the International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria. Fisher’s exact test, the Mann–Whitney U test, and McNemar’s test were used as appropriate. Results: Among the 26 evaluable patients (median age at initial diagnosis, 4.0 years [range, 1–10]; 20 boys [76.9%]), all had bone metastasis at enrollment, and MYCN amplification was detected in 6 of 21 patients with available data (28.6%). Tumor genomic profiling (24 patients) revealed alterations beyond MYCN, involving ALK, the RAS/MAPK pathway, DNA damage response genes, chromatin remodelers, and segmental copy-number changes, which informed matched targeted therapy in a subset of patients; atypical high-risk genomic alterations (ALK aberrations or RAS/MAPK pathway alterations) were present in 30.8% of the cohort, so that half of all patients carried MYCN amplification or an atypical high-risk alteration. The median number of prior chemotherapy courses was 14 (range, 5–23). The best ORR was 50.0% (13/26) and the DCR was 80.8% (21/26). The upgraded regimen group showed a numerically higher ORR (54.5% vs. 46.7%, P = 1.000) and DCR (90.9% vs. 73.3%, P = 0.356) than the original regimen group, with a lower proportion of progressive disease as best response (9.1% vs. 26.7%), although the differences were not statistically significant. In 21 patients with paired assessments, the ORR was 42.9% (9/21) after two cycles and 38.1% (8/21) after four cycles (P = 1.000); response conversion was bidirectional, with two of nine patients with partial response (PR) converting to complete response and three of nine patients with stable disease (SD) converting to PR, whereas two patients with PR and two with SD progressed. The interval from initial diagnosis to salvage treatment (approximated from age records) was not significantly associated with response, although patients whose best response was progressive disease showed a numerically longer interval (median, 3.0 vs. 2.0 years, P = 0.253). Conclusions: ATO-based salvage chemotherapy achieved an ORR of 50.0% and a DCR of 80.8% in heavily pretreated children with relapsed or refractory NB, with a higher DCR than in our previous salvage cohort. The upgraded regimen was associated with a numerical, but not statistically significant, improvement in disease control, mainly through a reduction in progressive disease. Because response conversion between the two-cycle and four-cycle assessments was bidirectional, response assessment after two cycles should be interpreted together with tolerability and the availability of alternative options rather than used as a sole basis for treatment switching. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective studies with larger cohorts.

items.title: Enhancing Clinical Classifier Robustness with Deep Representation Learning Based OOD Detection on DNA Methylation Data
items.abstract_or_text: DNA methylation (DNAM) array-based tumor classification is a powerful clinical diagnostic tool, but models trained on fixed reference cohorts can produce faulty predictions for tumor types not represented in the training distribution. We propose an end-to-end deep representation learning-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework for DNAm array data. Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers were trained on public sarcoma (SARC) (GSE140686) and brain tumor (BT) (GSE90496) cohorts, and feature vectors were extracted from bottleneck layers. Five OOD methods, including 1dimension (1D)-Subspace Analysis (1D-SSA), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Ridge Regression, Mahalanobis Distance (MD), and Sum of Squared Distances (SSD), were explored with 200 and 500-dimensional embeddings. Spectral discrepancy was used to discriminate in-distribution (IND) from OOD samples. Performance was measured via cross-validation, holdout samples, and an independent clinical dataset. 1D-SSA was the most effective approach. In the sarcoma-IND/brain tumor-OOD setting, the framework achieved an AUROC of 0.975 and True Negative Rate (TNR)@95TPR of 0.930, and an AUROC of 0.9569 and TNR@95TPR of 0.8660 for the brain tumor-IND/sarcoma-OOD setting. On the independent clinical test set, the method yielded a mean AUROC of 0.976, a DE of 0.032, an FPR@95TPR of 0.065, and a TNR@95TPR of 0.935. These results show deep representation-based OOD detection as a practical quality-control layer for clinical-grade methylation-based tumor classification systems.

items.title: A family-aware All of Us benchmark for polygenic prediction and genomic machine learning
items.abstract_or_text: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have improved substantially in predictive performance, yet results remain difficult to compare across studies that differ in cohorts, phenotype definitions, and evaluation procedures. Comparison to machine-learning methods is harder still, since their performance depends strongly on how data are partitioned and whether related individuals leak across splits. Here, we introduce a family-aware benchmark for polygenic prediction built on version 9 of the All of Us Research Program (AoU). The benchmark assigns entire family components to fixed discovery, calibration, and test partitions, reserves first-degree relatives for within-family evaluation, and separates models trained only on AoU discovery data from those using external GWAS summary statistics. This enables direct comparison between conventional PRS pipelines and machine-learning models trained under identical data budgets. We report results for 14 binary disease traits. Our strongest scores explain 5.7-24.9% of liability-scale variance, with particularly strong prediction for Alzheimer's disease, type 2 diabetes, prostate cancer, glaucoma, and inflammatory bowel disease, and match or exceed published commercial and academic scores for most traits. Across 12 traits with interpretable within-family estimates of within-sibship-to-population effect ratio, 11 confidence intervals included a ratio of 1. Type 2 diabetes showed an attenuation ratio of 0.86 [0.76, 0.97].

items.title: Deep Learning Based Cell Segmentation of 3D Confocal Images of Wood for Enzymatic Hydrolysis Applications
items.abstract_or_text: Plant cell walls are an abundant renewable resource for biobased products, but their recalcitrance limits enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Cell and tissue morphological parameters provide reliable biomarkers for predicting enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Accurate cell segmentation in 3D microscopy images is essential for quantifying these parameters. Although deep learning has achieved high performance in biological image segmentation, confocal microscopy's limited penetration depth leaves elongated wood cells partially imaged, creating open-ended structures that challenge existing segmentation methods. Based on an artificial longitudinal domain restriction, an adapted framework is presented here for the training of a 3D U-net model for the cell segmentation of wood images. Quantitative evaluation on a dedicated benchmark dataset identified a model configuration that reduced segmentation errors and produced more robust predictions during early enzymatic hydrolysis. These results support the use of the framework to quantify morphological parameters relevant to assessing and predicting biomass conversion efficiency.

items.title: A unified coarse-grained neural network potential for the dynamics of biomolecular complexes
items.abstract_or_text: The behavior of biomolecular complexes is governed by chemically specific interactions and often involves rare events that atomistic molecular dynamics struggle to capture within accessible timescales. Here we introduce AMARO v2.0, a coarse-grained neural network potential that retains all heavy atoms and treats solvent implicitly. Hydrogen-aware bead types and total-charge conditioning provide a shared representation for proteins, drug-like molecules, and their complexes, including ternary protein-protein-ligand systems. The model preserves folded proteins and captures key features of protein conformational free-energy landscapes. Across 262 complexes spanning 11 targets, the learned potential retains most ligand poses, although quaternary structure reorientation is observed for the HIF2A ternary complex. In targeted case studies, AMARO v2.0 distinguishes the two protonation states of trypsin-benzamidine and reaches the crystal binding pose in 3.3-fold more trajectories than all-atom molecular mechanics at a fixed estimated GPU-time budget. The same framework also recovers a reference binding pose in TYK2 and supports binding free-energy estimation for both trypsin-benzamidine and TYK2-EJM31, although the resulting values are more energetically favorable than the experimental references. SHP2 and CDK8 systems expose remaining limitations in binding-pose recovery and site specificity, respectively. Together, these results support AMARO v2.0 as a shared heavy-atom potential for biomolecular complex dynamics.

items.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

items.title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
items.abstract_or_text: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

items.title: Mimic: A Unified Neural Network Architecture for Modelling Genomic Sequences and Module-level Comparison
items.abstract_or_text: There exist a wide range of Neural Networks (NNs) that have modelled genomic sequences well. The architectures of these NNs consist of three steps: k-mer embedding, sequence embedding, and output mapping. The NNs are primarily differentiated from one another by their sequence embedding components. Although different NNs have been compared before, these comparisons are often either limited or involve drastically different NNs. Another issue is that some NNs are configured for a specific sequence length, and different length sequences require manual modification of the architectures. This study examines the architectures of established NNs for genomics sequences. Based on these architectures, a novel NN called Mimic is developed that provides a unified architecture for the principled comparison of NN components. Mimic was used to model two different types of genomic datasets: protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity. Along with other architecture components, different sequence embedding strategies were tried such as recurrent layers and convolutional layers. It was found that there exist specific NN components that yield significantly better performing models. Furthermore, Mimic significantly outperformed prevailing standard NNs, Bichrom and DeepSTARR, in modelling protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity, respectively. This study provides a framework for more extensive studies toward a general prescription of NN architecture for modelling genomics data.

items.title: An improved CRISPR-LICHT screen of 120 Tdark genes illuminates new biologically relevant SOX2 targets in human brain organoids
items.abstract_or_text: SOX2 is a transcription factor and central regulator of neural progenitor identity, yet the downstream molecular networks through which it supports human brain development remain incompletely characterized. Here, we applied CRISPR-lineage tracing at cellular resolution in heterogeneous tissue (CRISPR-LICHT) to human cerebral organoids to functionally interrogate SOX2-dependent regulatory networks. Using a SOX2-focused library targeting SOX2 together with conserved neurodevelopmental regulators expressed in neural progenitor cells, we showed that CRISPR-LICHT detects reproducible lineage- depletion phenotypes across genes already known to be involved in progenitor maintenance, fate specification, glial differentiation and neuronal maturation. This extends the application of CRISPR-LICHT beyond the severe neural progenitor phenotypes previously characterized for microcephaly-associated genes and demonstrates its ability to detect perturbation effects across a broader set of neurodevelopmental regulators, involving SOX2 targets previously defined in mouse and now open to further understanding in a human model setting. We further screened 120 evolutionarily conserved, poorly characterized SOX2-dependent genes classified as Tdark within the Illuminating the Druggable Genome framework and identified 28 candidate hits whose disruption impaired neural progenitor lineage expansion and/or survival. These candidates included proteins associated with cytoskeletal organization, membrane dynamics and intracellular architecture, suggesting that SOX2-dependent developmental programmes may engage cellular processes beyond transcriptional regulation. Individual downregulation of CDC42EP4, a poorly characterized CDC42 effector linked to cytoskeletal organization, revealed altered distribution of targeted progenitors between ventricular- and subventricular- like compartments, with changes consistent with altered progenitor-state progression. Together, these findings expand the functional landscape of SOX2-dependent regulation in human neural progenitors and identify cellular architecture as a potential component of SOX2-associated developmental programs.

items.title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging
items.abstract_or_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

items.title: Reliability-Aware Short-Term Glycemic Risk Prediction Using an Anchor-Based Comparative Framework of Sequence, Multimodal, and State-Updating Digital-Twin Models
items.abstract_or_text: Anticipating short-term hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic risk is essential for proactive diabetes management. However, existing machine learning approaches often use inconsistent evaluation protocols and emphasize predictive performance over reliability. This study introduces an anchor-based benchmarking framework integrating longitudinal glucose sequences and multimodal patient information. Using the T1DiabetesGranada dataset, 5,503,441 standardized prediction anchors were constructed from 736 individuals with type 1 diabetes to evaluate hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia prediction at 30-, 60-, and 120-minute horizons. Three neural architectures, a Hybrid LSTM-Transformer, a Multimodal Digital Twin, and a State-Updating Digital Twin with gap-aware longitudinal state progression, were compared under identical patient-level validation protocols. Beyond predictive performance, the evaluation examined calibration, classification thresholds, explanation reliability, cross-model disagreement, and robustness to controlled perturbations. No statistically significant predictive differences were observed after Holm correction, although the models exhibited complementary reliability characteristics. The Multimodal Digital Twin achieved the lowest mean Brier score, while the State-Updating Digital Twin demonstrated the lowest mean expected calibration error (ECE-10). The Hybrid LSTM-Transformer showed strong explanation faithfulness and stability under its temporal attribution protocol. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating digital-twin models beyond predictive accuracy and emphasize the need for reliability assessment and external validation before clinical deployment.
